title: Convert Your Jane Street Salary: Hourly to Annual Pay Guide
description: Use our hourly to annual calculator to estimate a Jane Street salary. Includes 38-hour week, fortnightly pay, tax, super, and minimum wage rates from Fair Work.

faqs.q: How do I convert an hourly rate to an annual salary for a Jane Street role?
faqs.a: Multiply your hourly rate by the number of hours you work each week, then multiply by 52. For a standard full‑time week of 38 hours, the formula is: hourly rate × 38 × 52. This gives your gross annual pay before tax and super. For example, an hourly rate of $100 becomes $197,600 per year. Use our [the timesheet](/) to try different hours.

faqs.q: Does the calculator include casual loading and superannuation?

The result shows both the annual gross and the estimated super contribution. See [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging) for more details.

faqs.q: What tax and Medicare deductions apply to a Jane Street salary?

bodyMarkdown:
## Understanding the Hourly to Annual Conversion

Converting an hourly wage to an annual salary is straightforward: multiply the hourly rate by the number of hours worked each week, then multiply by 52 weeks. For a full‑time employee, the standard week is 38 hours under the National Employment Standards. That means the annual gross pay equals the hourly rate × 38 × 52, or hourly rate × 1,976 hours.

If you are paid fortnightly, your gross pay is simply the weekly amount multiplied by two. For example, a $50 per hour rate gives $1,900 per week and $3,800 per fortnight. This conversion is useful when comparing job offers, such as a **jane street salary**, where the hourly rate may be quoted but you want to see the full‑year picture.

### Using the Timesheet Calculator

Our [the timesheet](/) lets you enter your base hourly rate and optionally add 25% casual loading. It then calculates weekly, fortnightly, monthly, and annual figures, along with estimated tax and super. The calculator assumes the same rate every week with no unpaid overtime, penalty rates, or allowances. For a precise determination of your pay, always refer to your award or enterprise agreement.

## National Minimum Wage and Award Rates

From 1 July 2026, the National Minimum Wage is $26.44 per hour for employees aged 21 and over. For a full‑time worker on 38 hours, that equals $1,004.90 per week. Casual employees receive a 25% loading, bringing their minimum to $33.05 per hour. These rates are set by the Fair Work Ombudsman and apply to award‑free employees.

Most employees are covered by a modern award, which specifies minimum pay rates for each classification. The Fair Work Commission publishes the Modern Awards Pay Database with detailed rates, allowances, and penalty rates. You can also find pay guides for each award on the Fair Work Ombudsman’s website. These guides include the minimum pay rates, monetary allowances, and the most frequently used penalty rates.

If you are curious about a **jane street salary**, note that such roles typically pay well above award rates. The conversion tool helps you compare any hourly offer to the annual equivalent, but always check the applicable award or enterprise agreement for your specific entitlements.

## Casual Loading and Superannuation

Casual employees are entitled to a 25% loading on top of the base hourly rate to compensate for not receiving paid leave. Our calculator includes a checkbox to add this loading automatically. The loading is applied to the hourly rate before calculating annual figures.

Superannuation is paid on top of your ordinary earnings. The super guarantee rate is 12% for 2026–27, and it applies up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830 per quarter. For example, if your annual gross pay is $100,000, the estimated super contribution is $12,000, paid by your employer into your super fund. This amount is not deducted from your take‑home pay. See [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging) for more details.

## Tax and Medicare

Your annual gross pay is subject to income tax and the Medicare levy. For the 2026–27 financial year, the resident tax rates are:

- Nil on the first $18,200
- 15% on income from $18,201 to $45,000
- 30% on income from $45,001 to $135,000
- 37% on income from $135,001 to $190,000
- 45% on income above $190,000

The Medicare levy is generally 2% of your taxable income. Our calculator uses the 2025–26 single reduction thresholds because the 2026–27 thresholds were not confirmed at the time of this guide. The result shows your estimated annual take‑home pay after tax and Medicare. For a high earner like a **jane street salary**, the top marginal rate of 45% plus 2% Medicare applies to income above $190,000.

Note that HELP repayments, the Medicare levy surcharge, and salary packaging are not included in this estimate. For a more detailed breakdown, visit our [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) page.

## Differences in Ordinary‑Time Earnings

The Australian Bureau of Statistics reports Average Weekly Earnings (AWE) for full‑time adult ordinary time at $2,083.70 per week (May 2026). That equates to an annual salary of about $108,352. For all employees (including part‑time), total earnings average $1,579.20 per week, or $82,118 annually. These figures help contextualise where a **jane street salary** sits relative to the broader market.

When using our calculator, remember that the annual figure is an estimate based on a consistent 38‑hour week. Actual earnings may vary due to overtime, penalty rates, allowances, or salary sacrifice. Always consult your pay slip and award for your exact entitlements.

## Using the Pay Guides and Reference Tables

Our [pay guides](/blog) page links to the official Fair Work Ombudsman pay guides for each award. You can also find historical pay rates and the [reference tables](/data) for minimum wages and allowances. These resources are essential for checking that your pay meets the legal minimums.

For a quick estimate of your annual pay from an hourly rate, start with [the timesheet](/) and adjust the hours if you work part‑time or casual. The calculator will show you the fortnightly, monthly, and annual figures, along with estimated tax and super. Remember that super is paid on top of your gross pay, not deducted from it.

Whether you are negotiating a **jane street salary** or checking your current award rate, understanding the hourly‑to‑annual conversion gives you confidence in your pay.
